title: Dario Amodei's stance on open weights is self-serving and short-sighted

content_html:
Jul 31, 2026 · 5 minutes to read

  • #tech
  • #machine learning

Leaders are often conflicted people. Marcus Aurelius wrote about the common humanity of all rational beings in “Meditations” while commanding invasions. Abraham Lincoln thought of slavery as morally wrong, yet his “paramount object” of preserving the Union made him initially resist immediate abolition.

In an interview with The Economist last week, Elon Musk said he can go “from exhilaration to terror regarding AI” during a single day. Dario Amodei seems to be conflicted as well. In his recent memo on open-weight AI models, the best of which are currently trained in China, he wrote in bold lettering that he had never advocated for a ban on them, yet in the very next sentence began adding asterisks to that statement. The New York Times reported last week that Anthropic privately lobbied for increased restrictions on Chinese open-weight AI models.

Dario Amodei writes that he only considers open-weight AI models that “don’t have dangerous capabilities” a public good. Later in the memo, he supports mandatory, government-organized safety testing for all sufficiently capable models, arguing that open-weight models are intrinsically harder to make safe because their safeguards can be removed. Proprietary models are inherently safer in his telling because their use is monitored and access to them can be withdrawn at any time. This line of thinking suggests that open weights are acceptable provided they remain below some government-defined capability threshold. If they are too capable, their use should be monitored or restricted, and since their use can’t be monitored, they should be curtailed by law.

Anthropic sells controlled access to centrally hosted models. A regulatory system built around expensive pre-release evaluations, continuous usage monitoring, identity verification, and revocable access naturally favours large providers of proprietary models. Anthropic already possesses the compliance, legal, and evaluation infrastructure needed to satisfy such a regime. A university lab, startup, or community does not, even if they somehow manage to train a sufficiently capable model.

Moreover, nominally applying the same test to closed and open-weight models is not genuinely symmetrical. Anthropic can control Claude’s safeguards. An open model must effectively be evaluated under its worst plausible modification because users can work around its built-in restrictions. The open model therefore faces an inherently harder standard. This fits the definition of regulatory capture: regulating the industry around the incumbent’s operating model while describing the rules as neutral.

Dario Amodei pays little attention to some of the main advantages of open-weight models. Companies and institutions can reliably run their own AI without relying on a handful of vendors with volatile policies and less-than-predictable billing and access conditions. Researchers can inspect, study (or at least try to), and fine-tune them.

Protectionism, especially restrictions on imports, will always reduce competitiveness and harm the companies it aims to “protect” as well as the country in the long term. If the current U.S. administration heeds the advice of Anthropic’s chief, the result will be a reduction in the West’s global competitiveness in AI and another step in ceding our civilizational dominance in this emerging technology. China will continue releasing new open-weight models, causing developers and tooling to adapt to an open Chinese stack instead of the restrictive and less competitive American offering.

Furthermore, export controls, for which Dario Amodei openly advocates, are already prompting China to build its own chips. China is, of course, behind the West, but not as much as you may think. Instead of adopting a Western technology stack and relying on our technology to build its AI models, China will increasingly rely on its own chips, reducing Western leverage.

Another of Dario Amodei’s proposed “crackdowns” targets “industrial-scale distillation”. He concedes that “distillation does not allow the CCP to obtain equivalent or superior AI capabilities to the US”, but argues that what matters is that it is “backed by an authoritarian state seeking to overtake the US at the frontier”. I understand his frustration that Chinese labs may be capturing some of his profits by offering cheap distillations of Claude. However, I think he shouldn’t dress up that (serious) commercial concern as the grander claim that Chinese AI will overtake the US by means of distillation.

I think Dario Amodei is sincerely afraid of a possible future danger from AI. I agree that there should be an industry or government body that briefly evaluates AI models before release, perhaps based on what Demis Hassabis has recently suggested. I also think the ideals of trust and safety on which Anthropic was founded are not fully thought through or perhaps not truly valued enough, and are thus crumbling under the pressure of power-seeking opportunism. This is evident in the current position and in previous hypocritical incidents, such as advocating for restrictions on the release of powerful AI models and then complaining when their AI model’s release has been restricted, billing users extra without documentation for having HERMES.md in recent commits, or claiming users will receive “free credits” to hide a significant price hike (estimated at 25×), which seems to have been paused after public outrage over the decision.

Amodei does not need to advocate an explicit ban on open weights. It is enough to establish a regulatory system in which only centrally hosted, monitored, and revocable models can be considered safe. That system would preserve frontier AI for companies such as Anthropic while ensuring that everyone else can access it only on those companies’ terms.

领导者往往是矛盾的人。 马可·奥勒留在指挥入侵时在《沉思录》中写到了所有理性存在的共同人性。 亚伯拉罕·林肯认为奴隶制在道德上是错误的，但他维护联邦的“首要目标”使他最初抵制立即废除奴隶制。

埃隆·马斯克上周在接受《经济学人》采访时表示，他可以在一天之内“对人工智能从兴奋变为恐惧”。 达里奥·阿莫代似乎也很矛盾。 在他最近关于开放权重人工智能模型的备忘录中，他用粗体字写道，他从未主张禁止这些模型，但在下一句话中开始在该声明中添加星号。 《纽约时报》上周报道称，Anthropic 私下游说加大对中国开放权重人工智能模型的限制。

达里奥·阿莫迪 (Dario Amodei) 写道，他只认为“不具有危险能力”的开放权重人工智能模型是公共产品。 在备忘录的后面，他支持对所有能力足够的模型进行强制性的、政府组织的安全测试，认为开放重量模型本质上更难确保安全，因为它们的防护措施可以被取消。 在他的讲述中，专有模型本质上更安全，因为它们的使用受到监控，并且可以随时撤回对它们的访问。 这种思路表明，只要开放权重低于政府定义的某些能力阈值，那么开放权重是可以接受的。 如果能力太强，就应该监控或限制其使用，既然无法监控，就应该通过法律限制。

Anthropic 出售对集中托管模型的受控访问。 围绕昂贵的预发布评估、持续使用监控、身份验证和可撤销访问建立的监管系统自然有利于大型专有模型提供商。 Anthropic 已经拥有满足这种制度所需的合规性、法律和评估基础设施。 大学实验室、初创公司或社区不会这样做，即使他们设法训练出一个足够强大的模型。

此外，名义上对封闭和开放重量模型应用相同的测试并不是真正对称的。 人择可以控制克劳德的防护。 开放模型必须在其最可能的修改下进行有效评估，因为用户可以绕过其内置限制。 因此，开放模型面临着本质上更严格的标准。 这符合监管捕获的定义：围绕现有企业的运营模式来监管行业，同时将规则描述为中立。

达里奥·阿莫代 (Dario Amodei) 很少关注开放重量模型的一些主要优点。 公司和机构可以可靠地运行自己的人工智能，而无需依赖少数政策不稳定且计费和访问条件难以预测的供应商。 研究人员可以检查、研究（或至少尝试）和微调它们。

保护主义，特别是对进口的限制，永远会降低竞争力，从长远来看会损害其旨在“保护”的企业以及国家。 如果现任美国政府听取人类首席执行官的建议，结果将是西方在人工智能领域的全球竞争力下降，并进一步放弃我们在这一新兴技术中的文明主导地位。 中国将继续发布新的开放权重模型，使开发人员和工具适应开放的中国堆栈，而不是限制性且竞争力较弱的美国产品。

此外，达里奥·阿莫迪公开倡导的出口管制已经促使中国制造自己的芯片。 当然，中国落后于西方，但并不像你想象的那么落后。 中国将不再采用西方技术堆栈并依靠我们的技术来构建人工智能模型，而是将越来越依赖自己的芯片，从而降低西方的影响力。

达里奥·阿莫迪提出的另一项“打击”目标是“工业规模蒸馏”。 他承认“蒸馏并不能让中共获得与美国相当或更好的人工智能能力”，但他认为重要的是它“得到了一个试图在边境超越美国的独裁国家的支持”。 我理解他的沮丧，因为中国实验室可能通过提供廉价的克劳德蒸馏物来获取他的部分利润。 然而，我认为他不应该将这种（严重的）商业担忧伪装成中国人工智能将通过蒸馏超越美国的宏大主张。

我认为达​​里奥·阿莫迪真诚地担心人工智能未来可能带来的危险。 我同意应该有一个行业或政府机构在发布之前对人工智能模型进行简要评估，也许是基于 Demis Hassabis 最近的建议。 我还认为，人类赖以建立的信任和安全理想没有得到充分考虑，或者可能没有得到足够的重视，因此在寻求权力的机会主义的压力下崩溃了。 这在目前的立场和之前的虚伪事件中很明显，例如主张限制强大的人工智能模型的发布，然后在其人工智能模型的发布受到限制时抱怨，在没有文件的情况下向用户收取额外费用，因为最近提交了 HERMES.md，或者声称用户将获得“免费积分”以隐藏大幅价格上涨（估计为 25 倍），但在公众对该决定感到愤怒后，这些行为似乎已暂停。

阿莫代不需要提倡明确禁止开放重量。 建立一个监管体系就足够了，在这个体系中，只有集中托管、监控和可撤销的模型才能被认为是安全的。 该系统将为 Anthropic 等公司保留前沿人工智能，同时确保其他人只能按照这些公司的条款访问它。
